Self-editing memory for agentic AI

How agents preserve, update, access, and manage their own context over multiple sessions.

Prashant Dhingra · Dataknobs slide guide · 35 slides

Explore the slidesRead the FAQ
OverviewFoundationsArchitectureGovernanceImplementationFAQSources
The essential idea

The model proposes. The runtime governs.

Self-editing memory is a model-guided process for managing external state. An agent selects pertinent facts and suggests modifications; application controls decide what can be stored, modified, accessed, or discarded. The objective is to ensure continuity across sessions with appropriate, up-to-date, and permitted context.

Design principle: enable agents to retain relevant context while ensuring enterprise control over policy, source authority, and lasting modifications.

This guide is based on the provided Dataknobs presentation, offering a textual explanation for each slide. The architecture, APIs, and rollout plans serve as illustrative examples, and the token comparisons are purely hypothetical.

01 / Foundations

Why agent memory needs a lifecycle

SLIDE 01

Self-editing memory for LLM and agentic AI systems

Agents can preserve valuable context over multiple sessions by choosing, updating, and accessing external memory. The key design criterion is to control these modifications during runtime.

SLIDE 02

A new contract between model and memory

The model suggests what should be remembered; the policy approves the modification, the store handles versioning, and the context compiler accesses it. Durable storage continues to be managed by the application.

SLIDE 03

Longer context is not always better context

Extensive transcripts can obscure decisions amid tool outputs, outdated plans, and temporary logs. Token limits, outdated assumptions, inefficient retrieval, and session resets drive the need for selective memory.

SLIDE 04

What self-editing memory means

Self-editing memory chooses lasting facts and suggests insert, replace, merge, or delete actions on external state. It does not alter model weights, bypass governance, or substitute authoritative source data.

SLIDE 05

From replaying history to maintaining state

Maintain a limited collection of essential facts, keep transcripts as reference material, and access pertinent information when needed. Compile only approved context for the specific task at hand.

SLIDE 06

Six complementary memory categories

Working memory maintains the present task state; core memory stores a few fixed facts; semantic memory contains facts and preferences. Episodic memory captures events, procedural memory includes established techniques, and archival memory safeguards source evidence.

02 / Architecture

Designing the memory service

SLIDE 07

Memory architecture

The architecture distinguishes between tiers, read operations, write operations, and compaction. Each layer possesses distinct persistence, retrieval, and control needs.

SLIDE 08

A fast, selective and durable memory hierarchy

L0 holds the active context window; L1 stores structured current facts; L2 offers searchable history; L3 retains raw evidence. The lower levels are accessed as needed rather than included in each prompt.

SLIDE 09

Enterprise reference architecture

Channels supply an agent framework equipped with a planner, tool router, context compiler, and evaluation hooks. A memory service oversees search, editing, consolidation, and approval within versioned storage, incorporating identity and tenant controls throughout all layers.

SLIDE 10

Context assembly at inference time

Comprehend intent, determine identity and scope, fetch candidates, reorder and validate, assign a token budget, then assemble the prompt. Implement authorization filters prior to ranking; the slide’s 64K budget serves as an example.

SLIDE 11

Memory writes as transactions

Examine a message or tool output, identify a potential fact, categorize it, resolve discrepancies, approve the modification, and save a versioned entry. An approved deployment change must replace the previous target and maintain proof.

SLIDE 12

Retrieval beyond similarity

Integrate namespace filters, precise lookup, keyword search, and vector retrieval. Rank candidates based on relevance, authority, recency, contradictions, and token cost; remove duplicates and keep source references.

SLIDE 13

Supersede instead of endlessly appending

When a deployment shifts from endpoint A to endpoint B, active retrieval must provide the most recent approved state. Previous versions stay connected as evidence, accompanied by an audit trail documenting approval.

SLIDE 14

Compaction without losing consequential facts

Maintain current goals, outstanding obstacles, and high-confidence limitations in the main context. Summarize finished tasks and store temporary logs; deleting information from an active prompt does not eliminate permanent records.

SLIDE 15

An auditable memory record

Store identity, namespace, owner, content, source, status, version, and supersession links. Retention, sensitivity, and consent dictate lifecycle decisions; version checks safeguard updates against concurrent modifications.

SLIDE 16

Shared memory and concurrency

Use distinct namespaces for organization, team, user, and session. When two agents read version 4 and one commits version 5, reject or reconcile the other agent’s outdated update rather than overwriting it silently.

03 / Governance

Trust, permission and assurance

SLIDE 17

Governance and assurance

Memory can affect future decisions and behaviors. Consider it a security-critical resource by implementing policy enforcement, human oversight, audit logs, and specialized assessments.

SLIDE 18

Three memory permission tiers

Protected policies are managed by their respective owners. Records of governed architecture and procedures are subject to mandatory review. Agent-controlled scratchpads may allow automatic modifications within specified limits and retention guidelines.

SLIDE 19

Memory poisoning

An untrusted page or message may insert a false rule that is subsequently accessed as trusted context. The risk lies in elevating low-trust input into persistent, high-trust memory.

SLIDE 20

Six control gates

Implement source provenance, read isolation, write validation, authorization, immutable auditing, and continuous assessment. These measures cover both data retrieval and storage; relying solely on a prompt instruction does not constitute a security boundary.

SLIDE 21

Human review of the actual change

Provide the authorized reviewer with the previous and proposed values, supporting evidence, scope, and version changes. Significant modifications must be clear, traceable, and reversible.

SLIDE 22

Memory as an observable data product

Document proposal, approval, update, retrieval, expiration, and reversal events. Monitor growth, outdated retrievals, conflict and reversal rates, unauthorized access, latency, and operational expenses.

SLIDE 23

Evaluate memory quality independently

Evaluate test retention over multiple sessions, update obsolete information, ensure authorized access, maintain evidence accuracy, resist poisoning attacks, and optimize efficiency. Integrate deterministic scenarios, adversarial examples, and vetted production samples.

SLIDE 24

Context cost and management overhead

The deck contrasts example input budgets of 80K tokens for transcript replay, 35K for RAG only, and 25K for governed memory. These numbers are illustrative, not benchmarks; indexing, review, storage, and evaluation introduce additional overhead.

04 / Implementation

From design to a controlled pilot

SLIDE 25

Implementation blueprint

The suggested framework is vendor-neutral and can be integrated into an agent harness. Begin with schema, permissioned APIs, orchestration boundaries, and phased rollout gates.

SLIDE 26

Proposed service and storage components

The example stack employs Next.js/Node for the frontend, an agent orchestrator, and Python/FastAPI to handle the memory service. PostgreSQL/JSONB, search or pgvector, object storage, and Redis or a queue fulfill various persistence and coordination functions.

SLIDE 27

Small, typed and permissioned memory tools

Make memory.search, memory.propose, memory.review, memory.commit, memory.history, and memory.expire accessible. Implement schemas, tenant scopes, rate limiting, idempotency, and expected-version validations on the server side.

SLIDE 28

Read, reason, propose and commit

Gather approved context, execute the agent, and then assess each suggested modification deterministically. Automatically apply only allowed changes; send other valid proposals for review. The model is not permitted to approve its own policy alterations.

SLIDE 29

Memory within the agent harness

Context compilation, limited tools, guardrails, evaluation, human oversight, and observability all encompass the agent. Memory governance functions within this broader feedback framework.

SLIDE 30

Governed memory in the Dataknobs portfolio

The deck outlines Kreate capabilities for persistent agents, Knobs experiments focused on retrieval and compression, and Kontrols oversight for approvals, rollback, and auditing. This represents a proposed capability map, not an official release announcement.

SLIDE 31

Coding and migration agents

Maintain documented architecture decisions, underlying causes, resolutions, and deployment results throughout sessions. Retain supporting evidence and refrain from considering a provisional diagnosis as a definitive conclusion.

SLIDE 32

Customer and finance assistants

The deck distinguishes low-risk display preferences from sensitive profiles that need review. Obtain up-to-date market and customer data from authorized systems of record; avoid relying on secrets or temporary prices as trusted sources.

SLIDE 33

A staged 90-day pilot

Days 0–30 focus on establishing schema, versioning, policy, and core APIs. Days 31–60 introduce retrieval, review, audit, and evaluation features. Days 61–90 involve connecting a single agent and comparing quality and cost in shadow mode. This timeline serves as a recommended plan.

SLIDE 34

Decisions for the architecture team

Determine ownership, writable classes, source authority, approval limits, expiration, evaluation, and the initial pilot. These decisions establish the product’s operating framework and risk parameters.

SLIDE 35

Sources and further reading

The deck mentions MemGPT, Letta, LangGraph, Anthropic, OWASP, and NIST. Its architecture diagrams, APIs, and roadmap serve as illustrative Dataknobs proposals; key primary-source reading links are provided below.

Questions, answered

Self-editing memory FAQ

What is self-editing memory in agentic AI?

Self-editing memory chooses lasting facts and suggests insert, replace, merge, or delete actions on external state. It does not alter model weights, bypass governance, or substitute authoritative source data.

Does self-editing memory change model weights?

No. In this setup, the agent suggests modifications to external records. Model training and fine-tuning occur as distinct processes.

How is memory different from RAG?

Retrieval-augmented generation incorporates pertinent evidence into a prompt. Self-editing memory introduces a process for proposing, reconciling, approving, versioning, and retiring lasting context; it may utilize retrieval as its read mechanism.

How should agents handle contradictory memories?

Evaluate the source’s authority, scope, and version. Replace outdated approved information with verified updates, maintain the origin, and forward unresolved material discrepancies for further review.

How do you reduce memory poisoning risk?

Implement source provenance, read isolation, write validation, authorization, immutable auditing, and continuous assessment. These measures cover both data retrieval and storage; relying solely on a prompt instruction does not constitute a security boundary.

Are the token savings in the deck measured results?

No. The token amounts of 80K, 35K, and 25K are merely hypothetical examples. Please verify task quality and overall operating cost using your own workloads.
